nameStory: The Audubon's Shearwater gets its name from the famous naturalist and bird artist John James Audubon, who first described and painted many North American birds in the 1800s. The word 'shearwater' comes from these birds' amazing flight technique - they skim so close to the ocean waves that they appear to 'shear' the water's surface with their wingtips. It's also called the Sargasso Shearwater because it often nests in areas near the floating Sargasso seaweed beds of the Atlantic.
description: The Audubon's Shearwater is a small seabird that spends most of its life flying over tropical and subtropical ocean waters. These graceful birds are built for life at sea, with long, narrow wings perfect for gliding just above the waves for hours without flapping. They're compact and streamlined, roughly the size of a small gull, with dark brownish-black backs and bright white undersides. In New England waters, spotting one is extraordinarily rare - like finding a tropical visitor far from home.

idTips.label: Flight Pattern
idTips.description: Flies with a distinctive 'shearing' motion, gliding on stiff wings just inches above the wave tops, banking steeply from side to side to show alternating dark back and white belly

idTips.label: Size and Shape
idTips.description: Compact seabird about the size of a small gull but with much longer, narrower wings and a more streamlined body built for ocean gliding

idTips.label: Coloration
idTips.description: Sharp contrast between dark brownish-black upperparts and clean white underparts, creating a striking two-toned appearance when banking in flight

idTips.label: Bill and Head
idTips.description: Small, dark, hooked bill typical of seabirds that catch fish, with dark cap extending below the eye and white throat

idTips.label: Habitat Behavior
idTips.description: Strictly oceanic - never seen on land except at remote nesting colonies, and rarely comes close to shore unless driven by storms

habitat: In New England waters, an Audubon's Shearwater would only be spotted far offshore in deep ocean waters, typically during warm summer months when tropical currents might carry one northward. These birds prefer warm ocean waters over the continental shelf and are most likely to be seen during pelagic birding trips many miles from shore. Any sighting would be extremely unusual, as they're tropical seabirds far outside their normal range.

seasonality.spring: Extremely unlikely to be seen, but any sightings would probably occur during late spring when warming ocean currents might occasionally bring tropical species northward.
seasonality.summer: The only season when a vagrant Audubon's Shearwater might possibly appear in New England waters, carried north by warm Gulf Stream currents during exceptionally warm years.
seasonality.fall: Virtually no chance of sightings as birds would be moving toward tropical wintering areas and away from northern waters.
seasonality.winter: No sightings expected - these tropical seabirds spend winter in warm southern waters far from New England's cold Atlantic.

funFact: Audubon's Shearwaters are so perfectly adapted to ocean life that their legs are positioned far back on their bodies, making them nearly helpless on land - they can barely walk and must shuffle on their bellies to move around their clifftop nesting burrows!
confusionNotes: Most likely to be confused with the Manx Shearwater, but Audubon's Shearwater is smaller, has a browner (not pure black) back, and shows less white extending up onto the face and neck area. Remember: 'Audubon's is Adorably small and brown-backed' versus the larger, starker black-and-white Manx.
contextualKnowledge: This species is sometimes called the 'Dusky-backed Shearwater' in older field guides, referring to its brownish-black (rather than pure black) upperparts. The scientific name honors French naturalist Félix Louis L'Herminier, but the common name Audubon's Shearwater can be confusing since Audubon actually painted the very similar Manx Shearwater, not this tropical species.
compareHints: Compared to its close relative the Manx Shearwater (the only other small shearwater you might see in New England), Audubon's Shearwater is noticeably smaller and more compact. The Manx has stark black upperparts and more extensive white on the face and sides of the neck, while Audubon's shows duller brownish-black above and less white extending up from the throat. Manx Shearwaters also have a more erratic, faster wingbeat pattern compared to Audubon's steadier gliding style.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Compared to its close relative the Sargasso Shearwater, the Manx Shearwater is noticeably larger with more contrasting black-and-white plumage - Sargasso Shearwaters are smaller, browner above rather than blackish, and have a more fluttery flight style.
